newsitem.title: ETHIOPIA: Kenya's bourse chief sees slower market growth.
newsitem.headline: Kenya's bourse chief sees slower market growth.

text.p: The Nairobi Stock Exchange will grow slower this year because of lower-than-expected economic growth in Kenya and cautious international investors, its chief executive said on Monday.
Job Kihumba told Reuters infrastructure problems, including poor roads and persistent power shortages, meant the cost of production was rising while profit margins were on the decline.

"Investors want to put money when they know profits will be higher, so they can gain from their investments. The situation is worrying, especially to foreign investors," he said on the fringes of an economic conference in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia.
Kihumba said the bourse, capitalised at around $1.8 billion, could only grow as fast as the general economy expanded and Kenya was not meeting its growth targets.

Kenya's gross domestic product growth was posted at 4.9 percent in 1995, 4.8 percent in 1996 and is pegged at around 4.5 percent in 1997. This compares with finance ministry forecasts of 5.0 percent, 6.0 percent and 7.0 percent respectively over the three-year period.
Kihumba said direct foreign investment had flattened out instead of increasing and the impact of poor infrastructure had dampened output by the agricultural and manufacturing sectors.
He added drought had exacerbated the situation.
"Drought means less coffee, less tea. Power shortages mean manufacturing is dampened. Companies are spending more on production, that does affect the market," he said.
Kihumba said foreign participation on the Nairobi bourse had risen to as much as 40 percent of daily trading in recent months but foreigners were careful about prices.
"It cannot be said that they manipulate the market; they just don't buy when prices rise to certain levels. We don't know why they don't want to pay more," he said.
He said shares at the Nairobi bourse were still very cheap, with price ratios of below 10, or even as in the case of Kenya Commercial Bank, below five.

He said the Nairobi market was still very thin and did not have enough participants at all levels. But he added that in Kenya wide share ownership was being encouraged hand-in-hand with institutional investment and high-net individuals.
The Nairobi Stock Exchange has 59 listed companies. The current primary share offer of Serena Lodges and Hotels, closing on April 14, will bring total listed companies to 60.

Kihumba said privatisations remained the main growth prospect for market liquidity at the Nairobi bourse. Kenyan authorities say Chemelil Sugar Co and Re-Insurance Corp will be listed sometime this year.

But Kihumba said the privatisation via the stock exchange of the giant Kenya Posts and Telecommunications Corp -- which employs 26,000 people -- and the Kenya Power and Lighting Co, were the only ones that would inject new life in the bourse.
"If investors put a billion dollars in Telekom (the would-be privatised telecommunications corporation), that would add growth impetus.
"We are looking at such privatisations, they are big enough to change direction of the market," he said.
Kihumba said it was the Nairobi Stock Exchange's view that restrictions on foreign investment did not serve any useful purpose and should be removed.
He said a central depository system (CDS) to speed up settlements was awaiting legislation.
